title: Fortifying a meal with dried, powdered oyster mushroom mycelium: Effects on postprandial metabolic parameters and on hunger and satiety regulation compared to a mushroom-free control meal in overweight/obese adults
summary:
Edible mushrooms, such as oyster mushrooms, are low in calories and high in dietary fiber—particularly β-glucans. These can increase feelings of fullness and positively influence glucose and fat metabolism after a meal, thereby helping to prevent overweight and obesity. Preliminary studies suggest that meals containing mushrooms or enriched with mushroom powder can reduce hunger and increase satiety.
In addition to the fruiting body, the mushroom’s mycelium is increasingly coming into focus. It is easy to cultivate and is considered a sustainable and forward-looking food ingredient. However, compared to the fruiting body, little is currently known about how mycelium influences metabolism and appetite-regulating processes.
The aim of the study is to investigate whether fortifying a meal with oyster mushroom mycelium, compared to a mycelium-free meal, affects sensations of hunger and satiety, as well as blood glucose and blood lipid levels and appetite-regulating hormones.

interventions.name: A standardized, energy-adjusted meal corresponding to 20% of the individual's total energy expenditure, with the addition of dried, powdered oyster mushroom mycelium (5 g per 100 kcal of the test meal)
standardized meal without oyster mushroom powder (control)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
BMI: 25.0–34.9 kg/m²; non-smoker (for at least 3 months)
Exclusion criteria:
Mushroom allergy or allergies, intolerances, or aversions to any components of the test meal or the second meal; known or imminent pregnancy or breastfeeding; planned lifestyle changes during the study period; current loss of appetite; known gastrointestinal diseases or disorders; known diabetes mellitus; presence of a pacemaker, defibrillator, or other implanted, automatic, electronic devices; skipping breakfast; eating disorders; use of fiber-containing dietary supplements as well as appetite suppressants or medications that may affect glucose and lipid metabolism or the regulation of food intake; use of antibiotics within the past 12 weeks; known intolerance to acetaminophen or regular use of acetaminophen; known liver disease or known abnormalities in liver and kidney function; drug use (substances controlled under the German Narcotics Act [BTMG] or other psychotropic substances); limited legal capacity; participation in another clinical trial; blood donation within 8 weeks prior to the start of the study and during the study
